title: HTTP cache lab: hit, revalidate or miss
objective: Predict whether a request hits the cache, revalidates with a 304, or goes to the origin, from its headers and its age.
summary: An intro video follows one stylesheet through a miss, a fresh hit and a stale revalidation with If-None-Match and 304. A simulation steps through request traces for seven header sets: max-age, no-cache, no-store, a heuristic lifetime, s-maxage at a CDN, Vary: Accept-Encoding, and hashed file names with immutable. A guided walkthrough loads each trace and pauses for predictions, and a summary video connects the cache key, the freshness check and revalidation.

scenes.heading: Fresh means lifetime is greater than age
At 90 seconds: stale, so ask first

watch.transcript:
# How a browser cache reuses one response

A browser asks for app.css. The first request misses and the cache stores the 200 response with max-age=60 and an ETag. At 30 seconds the copy is fresh and the cache answers alone. At 90 seconds the copy is stale, so the cache sends If-None-Match and the origin answers 304, which keeps the stored body.

**00:00 One stylesheet, one cache.** A cache keeps a copy of a response. Watch one browser cache reuse app.css.

**00:06 First request: a miss.** The first request finds no stored copy. The cache forwards it to the origin and stores the 200 response with its headers.

**00:16 Fresh means lifetime is greater than age.** A stored copy is fresh while its lifetime is greater than its age. Here max-age gives a lifetime of sixty seconds.

**00:26 At 30 seconds: a fresh hit.** At thirty seconds the age is thirty, so the copy is fresh. The cache answers alone, with no trip to the origin.

**00:35 At 90 seconds: stale, so ask first.** At ninety seconds the copy is stale. The cache asks the origin with If-None-Match. A 304 answer means keep your copy.

**00:46 304 or 200 after a revalidation.** A 304 sends only headers, so the cache reuses the stored body. A 200 sends a new body that replaces the copy.

Sources:

- RFC 9111: HTTP Caching — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111
- MDN Web Docs: HTTP and web networking — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP

guided.transcript:
# Change the cache headers and watch the outcome

The walkthrough steps through seven cache rules. max-age sets a lifetime; a stale copy revalidates with If-None-Match. no-cache stores but always revalidates, while no-store never stores. Without max-age a cache may guess about 10% of the time since Last-Modified. s-maxage gives shared caches such as a CDN their own lifetime. Vary keeps one copy per request header value. Hashed file names with a one-year max-age and immutable get a new cache key on every build.

**00:00 Change one header at a time.** Now change the headers yourself. Each scene loads a matching preset in the simulation beside the player.

**00:07 max-age=60 over two minutes.** With max-age set to sixty, requests at thirty and fifty-nine seconds are a HIT. At ninety seconds the copy is stale, so the cache must revalidate.

**00:19 Stale copy: If-None-Match, then 304.** The stale copy carries ETag v1. The cache sends If-None-Match v1. The origin answers 304, and the copy is fresh again.

**00:30 no-cache is not no-store.** no-cache stores the response but revalidates before every reuse. no-store never stores it, so every request goes to the origin.

**00:42 No max-age: a heuristic guess.** With no max-age and no Expires, a cache may guess a lifetime. A common guess is ten percent of the time since Last-Modified.

**00:53 s-maxage is for shared caches.** A CDN is a shared cache. For shared caches, s-maxage overrides max-age, so the CDN keeps the copy fresh for ten minutes.

**01:04 Vary: one copy per header value.** Vary Accept-Encoding makes the cache keep one copy per encoding. A gzip request cannot reuse the br copy.

**01:15 Hashed names: a new build is a new URL.** app.3f9a1c.js never changes, so it gets max-age of one year and immutable. A new build gets a new name, so a new cache key.

Sources:

- RFC 9111: HTTP Caching — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111
- MDN Web Docs: HTTP and web networking — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP
- Cloudflare developer documentation (DNS, Cache, Workers, Images) — https://developers.cloudflare.com/
- nodejs/undici: HTTP/1.1 client for Node.js (fetch, cache interceptor, cookies) — https://github.com/nodejs/undici

summary_video.title: Three questions decide every cached response
summary_video.blocker: FFmpeg is not installed and Docker is not running; install FFmpeg (for example `brew install ffmpeg`) or start Docker

scenes.heading: The cache asks in this order

summary_video.transcript:
# Three questions decide every cached response

A cache answers three questions in order: is there a stored copy for this key, is it fresh, and if not, does the origin answer 304 or 200. The directives set the answers: no-store, no-cache, max-age and s-maxage. A common pattern gives HTML no-cache with an ETag and hashed assets a one-year max-age with immutable.

**00:00 Three questions, every request.** Three questions decide every cached response. The cache asks them in the same order each time.

**00:06 The cache asks in this order.** First, is there a stored copy for this key? Second, is it fresh? Third, if stale, does the origin answer 304 or 200?

**00:18 Directives set the answers.** no-store means never store. no-cache means store, but check first. max-age gives seconds of freshness, and s-maxage does so for shared caches.

**00:30 HTML page versus hashed asset.** Give the HTML page no-cache and an ETag, so it is never stale. Give hashed assets a one-year max-age and immutable.

Sources:

- RFC 9111: HTTP Caching — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111
- MDN Web Docs: HTTP and web networking — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP

props.title: Cache decision per request: max-age=60

frames.caption: Request at 0 s. The cache has no copy of /app.css, so it asks the origin and stores the 200 response.
Request at 30 s. Lifetime 60 is greater than age 30, so the copy is fresh and the cache answers alone.
Request at 59 s. Lifetime 60 is still greater than age 59, so this is still a hit.
Request at 90 s. Age 90 is greater than lifetime 60, so the copy is stale. The cache sends If-None-Match: "v1", the origin answers 304, and the stored headers are updated.
Request at 120 s. The 304 at 90 s refreshed the copy, so its age is 30 and it is fresh again.
Request at 0 s. The cache has no copy of /app.css, so it asks the origin and stores the 200 response.
Request at 30 s. Lifetime 60 is greater than age 30, so the copy is fresh and the cache answers alone.
Request at 59 s. Lifetime 60 is still greater than age 59, so this is still a hit.
Request at 90 s. Age 90 is greater than lifetime 60, so the copy is stale. The cache sends If-None-Match: "v1", the origin answers 304, and the stored headers are updated.
Request at 120 s. The 304 at 90 s refreshed the copy, so its age is 30 and it is fresh again.
Request at 0 s. no-cache still lets the cache store the response, so it stores the 200 with ETag "v1".
Request at 10 s. no-cache means: validate before every reuse. The cache sends If-None-Match: "v1" and gets 304.
Request at 20 s. Again the cache asks first. The file is unchanged, so the origin answers 304 with headers only.
Request at 30 s. The file changed on the origin. If-None-Match: "v1" no longer matches, so the origin sends 200 with ETag "v2" and the new copy replaces the old one.
Request at 0 s. The response says no-store, so the cache must not store it. The origin answers.
Request at 10 s. There is still no stored copy, so the request goes to the origin again.
Request at 20 s. Every request with no-store is a full trip to the origin; nothing is reused.

heuristic.title: Cache decision per request: heuristic lifetime

frames.caption: Request at 0 h. No max-age and no Expires. The file was last modified 10 days ago. The cache stores the 200.

vars.headers: no max-age, Last-Modified 10 days ago, ETag "v1"

frames.caption: Request at 1 h. This cache uses the common heuristic: 10% of 10 days, about 24 hours. Age 1 h is less, so it is a hit.

vars.headers: no max-age, Last-Modified 10 days ago, ETag "v1"

frames.caption: Request at 23 h. The guessed lifetime of 24 h is still greater than the age, so it is a hit.

vars.headers: no max-age, Last-Modified 10 days ago, ETag "v1"

frames.caption: Request at 25 h. The copy is stale. The cache revalidates with If-None-Match: "v1" and gets 304. Another cache may guess differently.

vars.headers: no max-age, Last-Modified 10 days ago, ETag "v1"

s-maxage.title: Cache decision at a CDN: s-maxage=600

frames.caption: Request at 0 s reaches a CDN, a shared cache. It has no copy, so it asks the origin and stores the 200.
Request at 120 s. A browser cache would call this copy stale after 60 s. The CDN reads s-maxage=600, so its copy is fresh: a hit.
Request at 599 s. Age 599 is less than 600, so the CDN still answers alone.
Request at 700 s. The copy is stale. s-maxage also means the shared cache must revalidate once stale, so it sends If-None-Match: "v1" and gets 304.

vary.title: Cache decision per request: Vary: Accept-Encoding

frames.caption: Request at 0 s with Accept-Encoding: br. No copy for this key, so it is a miss. The cache stores the br copy.
Request at 10 s with Accept-Encoding: gzip. Vary says this header must match, and the br copy does not. Miss: the cache stores a gzip copy.
Request at 20 s with Accept-Encoding: br. It matches the br copy, which is 20 s old and fresh: a hit.
Request at 30 s with Accept-Encoding: gzip. It matches the gzip copy, which is 20 s old: a hit.

hashed.title: Cache decision per request: hashed file names

frames.caption: Day 0. The page asks for app.3f9a1c.js. No copy for this URL: a miss. The cache stores it with a one-year lifetime.
Day 1. Same URL, age 1 day, lifetime 1 year: a hit with no trip to the origin.
Day 30. Still a hit. The file at this URL never changes, so a long lifetime is safe.
Day 31, after a deploy. The HTML now names app.8b2e7d.js. A new URL is a new cache key, so there is no stored copy: a miss, then one fetch.

checkpoints.prompt: In one sentence: why could the cache answer at 30 seconds without asking the origin?
checkpoints.explanation: The copy was fresh: its lifetime from max-age=60 was greater than its age of 30 seconds. A fresh copy may be reused with no request to the origin.

checkpoints.prompt: The copy has max-age=60 and ETag "v1" and is now 90 seconds old. The file has not changed. What happens?

choices.text: The cache sends If-None-Match: "v1" and the origin answers 304
The cache serves the copy, because it still has one
choices.misconception: Thinks a stored copy can be reused at any age

choices.text: The cache deletes the copy and downloads the whole file again
choices.misconception: Thinks stale means unusable, ignoring validation with the ETag

checkpoints.explanation: A stale copy needs validation before reuse. The cache sends the stored ETag in If-None-Match. The file is unchanged, so the origin answers 304 and the cache keeps the stored body.

checkpoints.prompt: An HTML page says Cache-Control: no-cache and has an ETag. What does the browser do on the next visit?

choices.text: It uses its stored copy only after the origin answers 304
It never stores the page, so it downloads the full page
It serves the stored page without asking
choices.misconception: Thinks no-cache is ignored when a copy exists

checkpoints.explanation: no-cache lets a cache store the response but forbids reuse without validation. The browser sends If-None-Match, and a 304 lets it reuse the stored page. Only no-store forbids storing.

checkpoints.prompt: In the simulation, step to the request that misses even though the old file is cached for a year. Which URL does it ask for?

goal.hint: Press Forward until the day 31 request after the deploy.

checkpoints.explanation: The cache key includes the URL. A new build gets a new hashed name, so the cache has no stored copy for it and must fetch it once. The year-long lifetime of the old URL does not matter.

checkpoints.prompt: Load the Vary preset and step until the cache holds two copies of the same URL. Which request header made the second copy?

goal.hint: Press Forward once, to the gzip request at 10 seconds.

checkpoints.explanation: Vary: Accept-Encoding says the stored response fits only requests with the same Accept-Encoding. The gzip request does not match the br copy, so the cache misses and stores a second copy.

checkpoints.prompt: A response says max-age=60, s-maxage=600. At 120 seconds, which cache still serves it as fresh?

choices.misconception: Thinks s-maxage replaces max-age for every cache

checkpoints.explanation: Only shared caches read s-maxage, and for them it overrides max-age. The browser cache uses max-age=60, so its copy is stale at 120 seconds. The CDN copy is fresh until 600 seconds.
